Judith Leyster. The Dutch Golden Age painter renowned for her intimate domestic scenes, flirtations, and music-making moments rendered with warm light and psychological nuance. She achieved independent professional standing in Haarlem—rare for women. And her rediscovery in the twentieth century corrected centuries of attribution errors that buried her as a student of Hals.

Her Self-Portrait from around 1635 shows her at the easel, palette in hand, turning to the viewer with confident directness. A rare claim of artistic authority by a woman in her era. Leyster specialized in tronies—character studies—and genre scenes. The Jolly Topers, A Young Man Playing a Flute, Two Men Offering Oysters to a Young Woman. Domestic moments animated by flirtation and music.

Her brushwork echoes Frans Hals' spontaneity and warmth. But her palette is often more golden and her interiors more detailed. The attribution question between Hals and Leyster has been a scholarly thriller. Is this Hals or Leyster? A question that mirrors the broader erasure of women artists' autonomy.

Leyster married Jan Miense Molenaer, also a painter, in 1636. She largely ceased signing her work afterwards. A loss both professional and to history. Many of her paintings were attributed to him for centuries. Her rediscovery began in 1893 when a scholar noticed a monogram beneath old varnish on works thought to be early Hals. Modern conservation revealed dozens of paintings wrongly attributed to male peers.

She worked professionally in Haarlem's guild and commanded high prices for her portraits and genre paintings. She owned her own studio and took students. Unusual independence for a woman painter. Her work bridges Frans Hals' gestural freedom with a warmer, more intimate register. Her scenes feel lived-in and affectionate rather than theatrical. She stands alongside Artemisia Gentileschi as a pioneering figure in breaking gender barriers in professional art.
